concepts.title: Social Groups: Aggregate, Category and Quasi-Group

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Social Groups: Aggregate, Category and Quasi-Group' refers to.
questions.a: A social group exists only where people interact regularly, share a sense of belonging and define themselves as members. Mere gatherings and mere collections of similar people are not groups: an aggregate is people physically together (a bus queue), a category is people alike in some trait (all tall persons), and a quasi-group has common interests but no organisation yet.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Social Groups: Aggregate, Category and Quasi-Group'.
questions.a: Interaction plus membership feeling makes a group -- not proximity, not similarity alone.

concepts.title: Status and Role: Ascribed and Achieved

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Status and Role: Ascribed and Achieved' refers to.
questions.a: Status is a person's position in a social system, carrying honour or rank; role is the behaviour expected of whoever occupies that status. Some statuses are ascribed at birth -- caste, sex, royal birth -- while achieved statuses are earned through effort, and each person holds a whole cluster of statuses at once.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Status and Role: Ascribed and Achieved'.
questions.a: You occupy a status and perform its role -- some statuses are given at birth, others are earned.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Status and Role: Ascribed and Achieved' taught, and from which source text?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Social Control, Society and Community' refers to.
questions.a: Society is the largest web of relationships marked by self-sufficiency and continuity, while a community is a smaller grouping held by locality and a feeling of belonging. Neither survives by goodwill alone: norms backed by sanctions -- folkways, mores and laws -- exert social control, rewarding conformity and punishing deviation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Social Control, Society and Community'.
questions.a: Norms are the traffic rules of social life -- sanctions, soft or hard, keep everyone on the road.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Culture: Nature versus Nurture' refers to.
questions.a: Culture is the learned, shared design of living -- beliefs, values, practices and artefacts -- that distinguishes human groups. The nature versus nurture debate asks how much of behaviour is biological instinct and how much cultural learning; sociology stresses nurture, showing how the same biological needs are satisfied in strikingly different ways across cultures.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Culture: Nature versus Nurture'.
questions.a: Humans are born unfinished -- culture completes us, teaching what nature never specified.
